'''''There Will Be Blood''''' is a 2007 American [[epic film|epic]] [[period drama film]] co-produced, written and directed by [[Paul Thomas Anderson]], loosely based on the 1927 novel ''[[Oil!]]'' by [[Upton Sinclair]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://explore.bfi.org.uk/sightandsoundpolls/2012/film/4ce2b8c6518bb|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120820043758/http://explore.bfi.org.uk/sightandsoundpolls/2012/film/4ce2b8c6518bb|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 20, 2012|title=There Will Be Blood (2007)|publisher=[[The British Film Institute]]}}</ref> It stars [[Daniel Day-Lewis]], [[Paul Dano]], [[Kevin J. O'Connor (actor)|Kevin J. O'Connor]], [[Ciarán Hinds]], and [[Dillon Freasier]]. The film follows [[silver miner]]-turned-oilman Daniel Plainview (Day-Lewis) as he embarks on a ruthless quest for wealth during the [[History of oil in California through 1930|Californian oil boom]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Development on ''There Will Be Blood'' began after writer [[Eric Schlosser]] purchased the film rights to Sinclair's novel in 2004. It was acquired by [[Ghoulardi Film Company]], [[Paramount Vantage]] and [[Miramax Films]] after Anderson completed the first draft of the film's screenplay. Day-Lewis immediately joined the project while Dano, who initially signed on for a smaller role, took on a starring role after replacing [[Kel O'Neill]] during filming. [[Principal photography]] began in June 2006 and lasted until that September, with filming locations including Los Angeles and [[Marfa, Texas]]. The film's music was composed by [[Radiohead]] guitarist [[Jonny Greenwood]].

''There Will Be Blood'' premiered at [[Fantastic Fest]] in [[Austin, Texas|Austin]] on September 29, 2007. It was first theatrically released in New York City and Los Angeles on December 26 and in selected international markets on January 25, 2008. It grossed $76.2&nbsp;million worldwide and received acclaim from critics, with praise for the cinematography, Anderson's direction and screenplay, music, and performances of Day-Lewis and Dano. The [[National Board of Review: Top Ten Films#2000s|National Board of Review]], the [[American Film Institute Awards 2007|American Film Institute]] and the [[National Society of Film Critics]] named ''There Will Be Blood'' one of the top-ten films of 2007. The film was nominated for eight awards at the [[80th Academy Awards]], winning two ([[Academy Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] for Day-Lewis and [[Academy Award for Best Cinematography|Best Cinematography]] for [[Robert Elswit|Elswit]]) and received numerous [[There Will Be Blood#Accolades|other accolades]]. It topped various lists of the best films of the 2000s and was Anderson's best-reviewed film until 2025's ''[[One Battle After Another]]''.
== Plot ==
<!-- Per WP:FILMPLOT, plot summaries should be 400-700 words for feature films -->
In 1898, Daniel Plainview finds silver while prospecting in [[New Mexico Territory|New Mexico]] but breaks his leg. Dragging himself from the pit, he takes a sample to an [[assay office]] and receives a silver and gold [[land claim|claim]]. In 1902, [[history of oil in California through 1930|he discovers oil in California]]. Following the death of a worker in an accident, Daniel adopts his orphaned son, H.W., in order to pass himself off as a family man to potential investors.

In 1911, Daniel is approached by Paul Sunday, a young man who tells him of an oil deposit in Little Boston. Daniel visits the Sundays' property in Little Boston and meets Paul's twin brother Eli, a preacher. Daniel attempts to purchase the farm from the Sundays at a bargain price under the ruse of using it to hunt quail, but his motives are questioned by Eli, who knows the land has oil. In exchange for the property, Eli demands $10,000 for his church. Plainview counters with a $5,000 offer, and an agreement is made and Daniel acquires all the available land in and around the Sunday property, except for the land owned by one holdout, William Bandy.

After Daniel reneges on an agreement to let Eli bless the well before drilling begins, a series of misfortunes occur: an accident kills one worker and a [[blowout (well drilling)|gas blowout]] deafens H.W. and destroys the drilling infrastructure. When Eli publicly demands the money still owed to him, Daniel beats and humiliates him. At the dinner table that night, Eli attacks and berates his father for having trusted Daniel.

A man arrives at Daniel's doorstep, claiming to be his half-brother, Henry. Later that night, H.W. sets fire to their shack. Daniel chases, restrains, and then sends H.W. to a school for the deaf in San Francisco. 

[[Standard Oil]] offers to buy out Daniel's local interests, but Daniel refuses and instead strikes a deal with [[Union Oil]] to build a pipeline. However, Bandy's ranch remains an impediment.

Daniel becomes suspicious of Henry after he fails to recognize a childhood joke and confronts him one night at gunpoint. "Henry" confesses that he was a friend of the real Henry, who died of [[tuberculosis]], and that he had impersonated Henry in the hope that Daniel could give him a job. An enraged Daniel murders him and buries his body. After looking through the real Henry's journal that the imposter Henry had with him revealing that the real Henry was traveling to meet him, Daniel drinks and weeps. The next morning, Daniel is awakened by Bandy, who knows of Daniel's crime and wants him to publicly repent in Eli's church in exchange for an [[easement]] to run his pipeline across the ranch. As part of his [[baptism]], Eli humiliates Daniel and coerces him into confessing that he abandoned his child. Later, while the pipeline is being built, H.W. reunites with Daniel and Eli becomes a missionary.

In 1927, H.W. marries Paul and Eli's sister Mary. Daniel, now extremely wealthy but an alcoholic, lives alone in a large mansion. H.W. asks his father to dissolve their partnership so that he can move to Mexico with Mary and start his own drilling company. Daniel angrily mocks H.W.'s deafness before revealing his true origins and disowning him as his son. H.W. leaves after thanking God he is not related to Daniel. 

Eli, now a radio preacher, visits a drunken Daniel in the [[bowling alley]] in his basement. Eli asks Daniel to partner with the church in drilling Bandy's property. Daniel agrees on the condition that Eli denounce his faith. Once Eli acquiesces, Daniel reveals that he already drained the property of its oil supply by [[Rule of capture|capture]] and taunts Eli for his misfortune in investments he made [[Wall Street crash of 1929|when the market crashed]]. Daniel torments Eli further by telling him a lie about how he gave his brother $10,000 instead and is now a wealthy man. He chases Eli around the alley and bludgeons him to death with a bowling pin. When his butler appears to investigate the commotion, Daniel announces, "I'm finished."

== Themes and analysis ==
Critics see the film as a commentary on the nature of [[capitalism]] and greed, and its inherent national presence in America.<ref>{{cite web |title=There Will Be Blood: The madness of American capitalism...but no method |url=https://freepress.org/article/there-will-be-blood-madness-american-capitalismbut-no-method |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181023120026/http://freepress.org/article/there-will-be-blood-madness-american-capitalismbut-no-method |archive-date=October 23, 2018 |access-date=January 11, 2017}}</ref> [[David Denby]] of ''[[The New Yorker]]'' described the film as being about "the driving force of capitalism as it both creates and destroys the future" and goes on to say that "this movie is about the vanishing American frontier. The thrown-together buildings look scraggly and unkempt, the homesteaders are modest, stubborn, and reticent, but, in their undreamed-of future, [[Wal-Mart]] is on the way."<ref>{{cite magazine |date=December 10, 2007 |title=Hard Life |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2007/12/17/hard-life-2-2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170207051250/http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2007/12/17/hard-life-2-2/ |archive-date=February 7, 2017 |access-date=January 11, 2017 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> Daniel Plainview's "I have a competition in me" speech has been looked upon as important when analyzing the film from this angle.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Critical Analysis of There Will Be Blood: Intensional Godhood – Noisewar Internetlainen |url=http://warandnoise.com/therewillbeblood/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170124194218/http://warandnoise.com/therewillbeblood/ |archive-date=January 24, 2017 |access-date=January 11, 2017}}</ref>

Others have noted themes of faith, religion, and family.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.unomaha.edu/jrf/vol12no2/Reviews/ThereWillBBlood.htm|title=University of Nebraska Omaha|access-date=January 11, 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910033735/http://www.unomaha.edu/jrf/vol12no2/Reviews/ThereWillBBlood.htm|archive-date=September 10, 2015}}</ref> James Christopher of ''The Times'' viewed the film as "a biblical parable about America's failure to square religion and greed."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nonesuch.com/journal/times-uk-evening-standard-give-there-will-be-blood-five-stars|title=Nonesuch Records Times (UK), Evening Standard Give "There Will Be Blood" Five Stars|date=February 11, 2008 |access-date=January 11, 2017|archive-date=June 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160617014657/http://www.nonesuch.com/journal/times-uk-evening-standard-give-there-will-be-blood-five-stars|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Production ==
=== Development ===
[[File:Paul Thomas Anderson & Daniel Day-Lewis-2.jpg|thumb|right|[[Paul Thomas Anderson]] and [[Daniel Day-Lewis]] in New York, December 2007.]]
After [[Eric Schlosser]] finished writing ''[[Fast Food Nation]]'', many reporters noted similarities to Upton Sinclair's book ''[[The Jungle]]''. Although Schlosser had not read the book and was unfamiliar with Sinclair's other works, comparisons between the two books prompted Schlosser to read Sinclair's works, including the novel ''[[Oil!]]''. Schlosser, who found the book to be exciting and thought it would make an excellent film, sought out the Sinclair estate and purchased the film rights. Schlosser intended to find a director who was as passionate about the book as he was but director [[Paul Thomas Anderson]] approached him first.<ref name="ES-TNYT-2008">{{cite news |author-last1=Schlosser|author-first1= Eric |date=February 22, 2008 |title='Oil!' and the History of Southern California |newspaper=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/02/22/timestopics/topics_uptonsinclair_oil.html}}</ref>

Anderson had an existing screenplay about two fighting families. He struggled with the script and soon realized it was not working.<ref name="Stern">{{cite news |author-last1=Stern|author-first1= Marlow |title='There Will Be Blood' Press Conference |work=Manhattan Movie Magazine |date=December 10, 2007 }}</ref> Homesick while away in London, Anderson purchased a copy of ''Oil!'', drawn to its cover illustration of a California oilfield.<ref name="Goodwin">{{cite news |author-last1=Goodwin|author-first1= Christopher |title=Daniel Day-Lewis Gives Blood, Sweat and Tears |newspaper=The Sunday Times |date=November 25, 2007 |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/film/article2922563.ece |access-date=December 21, 2009 |location=London |archive-date=May 17, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110517072924/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/film/article2922563.ece |url-status=dead }}</ref> Inspired by the novel, Anderson contacted Schlosser and adapted the first 150 pages to a screenplay. Research trips to museums dedicated to early oilmen in [[Bakersfield]] assisted Anderson in the development of the screenplay.<ref name="Hirschberg">{{cite news |author-last1=Hirschberg|author-first1= Lynn |title=The New Frontier's Man |newspaper=The New York Times Magazine |date=December 11, 2007 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/11/magazine/11daylewis-t2.html?_r=2&adxnnl=1&oref=slogin&adxnnlx=1197697066-ZGxe5I9RiTtwkgTydXd2Dg&oref=slogin |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-date=September 19, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110919060126/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/11/magazine/11daylewis-t2.html?_r=2&adxnnl=1&oref=slogin&adxnnlx=1197697066-ZGxe5I9RiTtwkgTydXd2Dg&oref=slogin |url-status=live }}</ref> Anderson changed the title from ''Oil!'' to ''There Will Be Blood'' because he felt "there's not enough of the book [in the film] to feel like it's a proper adaptation".<ref name="Stern" />

He said of writing the screenplay:
{{blockquote|I can remember the way that my desk looked, with so many different scraps of paper and books about the oil industry in the early 20th century, mixed in with pieces of other scripts that I'd written. Everything was coming from so many different sources. But the book was a great stepping-stone. It was so cohesive, the way Upton Sinclair wrote about that period, and his experiences around the oil fields and these independent oilmen. That said, the book is so long that it's only the first couple hundred pages that we ended up using, because there is a certain point where he strays really far from what the original story is. We were really unfaithful to the book. That's not to say I didn't really like the book; I loved it. But there were so many other things floating around. And at a certain point, I became aware of the stuff he was basing it on. What he was writing about was the life of [oil barons] [[Edward Doheny]] and [[Harry Ford Sinclair|Harry Sinclair]]. So it was like having a really good collaborator, the book.<ref name="Modell">{{cite web |last=Modell |first=Josh |title=Paul Thomas Anderson |url=https://www.avclub.com/paul-thomas-anderson-1798213013 |work=The A.V. Club |access-date=September 2, 2012 |date=January 2, 2008 |archive-date=August 23, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120823131730/http://www.avclub.com/articles/paul-thomas-anderson%2C2120/ |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

Anderson, who had said that he would like to work with Daniel Day-Lewis,<ref name="Patterson">{{cite news |author-last1=Patterson|author-first1= John |title='Magnolia' Maniac |newspaper=The Guardian |date=March 10, 2000 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2000/mar/10/culture.features |access-date=April 12, 2010 |location=London |archive-date=August 27, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120827044550/http://www.guardian.co.uk/film/2000/mar/10/culture.features |url-status=live }}</ref> wrote the screenplay with Day-Lewis in mind and approached Day-Lewis when the script was nearly complete. Anderson had heard that Day-Lewis liked his earlier film ''[[Punch-Drunk Love]]'', which gave him the confidence to hand Day-Lewis a copy of the incomplete script.<ref name="LATimesLewis">{{cite news |title=Prospectors Anderson and Day-Lewis Strike Black Gold |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=December 19, 2007 }}</ref> According to Day-Lewis, being asked to do the film was enough to convince him.<ref name="Freydkin">{{cite news |author-last1=Freydkin|author-first1= Donna |title=Daniel Day-Lewis has recognition in his 'Blood' |newspaper=USA Today |date=December 10, 2007 |url=https://www.usatoday.com/life/people/2007-12-10-blood-premiere_N.htm |access-date=December 21, 2007 |archive-date=January 18, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080118234131/http://www.usatoday.com/life/people/2007-12-10-blood-premiere_N.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> In an interview with ''[[The New York Observer]]'', he elaborated that what drew him to the project was "the understanding that [Anderson] had already entered into that world, [he] wasn't observing it {{ndash}} [he'd] entered into it {{ndash}} and indeed [he'd] populated it with characters [who he] felt had lives of their own".<ref name="Vilkomerson">{{cite news |author-last1=Vilkomerson|author-first1= Sarah |title=P.S. I Love You Daniel Day-Lewis |newspaper=New York Observer |date=December 18, 2007 |url=http://www.nyobserver.com/2007/sara-vilkomerson-s-guide-week-s-movies-p-s-i-love-you-daniel-day-lewis |access-date=December 31, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071225010901/http://www.nyobserver.com/2007/sara-vilkomerson-s-guide-week-s-movies-p-s-i-love-you-daniel-day-lewis |archive-date=December 25, 2007 }}</ref>

Anderson said that the line in the final scene, "I drink your [[milkshake]]!", was paraphrased from a quote by former Secretary of the Interior and [[U.S. Senator]] from [[New Mexico]], [[Albert Fall]], speaking before a Congressional investigation into the 1920s oil-related [[Teapot Dome scandal]]. Anderson said he was fascinated "to see that word [milkshake] among all this official testimony and terminology" to explain the complicated process of oil drainage.<ref>{{cite news |author-last1=Foundas|author-first1= Scott |date=January 16, 2008 |url=http://www.laweekly.com/2008-01-17/film-tv/blood-sweat-and-tears |title=Paul Thomas Anderson: Blood, Sweat and Tears |newspaper=LA Weekly |access-date=May 25, 2010 |archive-date=June 29, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629141136/http://www.laweekly.com/2008-01-17/film-tv/blood-sweat-and-tears/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2014, an independent attempt to locate the statement in Fall's testimony proved unsuccessful—an article published in the ''Case Western Reserve Law Review'' suggested that the actual source of the paraphrased quote may instead have been remarks in 2003 by Sen. [[Pete Domenici]] of New Mexico during a debate over drilling in the [[Arctic National Wildlife Refuge]].<ref>{{cite web |author-first1=Peter M. |author-last1=Gerhart |author-first2= Robert D. |author-last2=Cheren |url=http://law.case.edu/journals/LawReview/Documents/63CaseWResLRev4.4.Article.GerhartCheren.pdf |title=Recognizing the Shared Ownership of Subsurface Resource Pools |publisher=63 Case W. Res. L. Rev. 1041, 1047 n.9 (2014) |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131104184051/http://law.case.edu/journals/LawReview/Documents/63CaseWResLRev4.4.Article.GerhartCheren.pdf |archive-date=November 4, 2013 }}</ref> In those remarks, Domenici stated:<ref>149 Cong. Rec. 6729 (2003).</ref>

{{Blockquote|The oil is underground, and it is going to be drilled and come up. Here is a giant reservoir underground. Just like a curved straw, you put it underground and maneuver it, and the 'milk shake' is way over there, and your little child wants the milk shake, and they sit over here in their bedroom where they are feeling ill, and they just gobble it up from way down in the kitchen, where you don't even have to move the Mix Master that made the ice cream for them. You don't have to take it up to the bedroom. This describes the actual drilling that is taking place.}}

According to Joanne Sellar, one of the film's producers, the film was difficult to finance because "the studios didn't think it had the scope of a major picture".<ref name="Goodwin" /> It took two years to acquire financing for the film.<ref name="Hirschberg" /> For the role of Plainview's "son", Anderson looked at people in Los Angeles and New York City, but he realized that they needed someone from [[Texas]] who knew how to shoot shotguns and "live in that world".<ref name="Stern" /> The filmmakers asked around at a school and the principal recommended [[Dillon Freasier]]. They did not have him read any scenes and instead talked to him, realizing that he was the perfect person for the role.<ref name="Stern" />

To build his character, Day-Lewis started with the voice. Anderson sent him recordings from the late 19th century to 1927 and a copy of the 1948 film ''[[The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (film)|The Treasure of the Sierra Madre]]'', including documentaries on its director, [[John Huston]], an important influence on Anderson's film.<ref name="Goodwin" /> According to Anderson, he was inspired by the fact that ''Sierra Madre'' is "about greed and ambition and paranoia and looking at the worst parts of yourself."<ref name="Hirschberg" /> While writing the script, he would put the film on before he went to bed at night. To research for the role, Day-Lewis read letters from laborers and studied photographs from the time period. He also read up on oil tycoon [[Edward Doheny]], upon whom Sinclair's book is loosely based.<ref name="Lewis">{{cite news |author-last1=Lewis|author-first1= Judith |title=Daniel Day-Lewis: The Way He Lives Now |newspaper=L.A. Weekly |date=December 19, 2007 |url=http://www.laweekly.com/film+tv/film/daniel-day-lewis-the-way-he-lives-now/17906 |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071223021614/http://www.laweekly.com/film+tv/film/daniel-day-lewis-the-way-he-lives-now/17906 <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=December 23, 2007}}</ref>

=== Filming ===
[[Principal photography]] began in June 2006 on a ranch in [[Marfa, Texas]],<ref name="Hirschberg" /> and took three months.<ref name="Goodwin" /> Other location shooting took place in Los Angeles. The film was shot using [[Panavision]] XL [[35mm movie film|35 mm]] cameras outfitted primarily with Panavision C series and high-speed [[anamorphic]] lenses.<ref name="DigContentProducer">{{cite web |last=Goldman |first=Michael |date=November 1, 2007 |title=Old-Fashioned Filmmaking |url=https://digitalcontentproducer.com/mil/features/video_oldfashioned_filmmaking/index2.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080322200054/http://digitalcontentproducer.com/mil/features/video_oldfashioned_filmmaking/index2.html |archive-date=March 22, 2008 |access-date=February 24, 2008}}</ref> Anderson tried to shoot the script in sequence with most of the sets on the ranch.<ref name="Hirschberg" />

Two weeks in, Anderson replaced the actor playing Eli Sunday ([[Kel O'Neill]]) with [[Paul Dano]], who had originally been cast only in the much smaller role of Paul Sunday, the brother who tipped off Plainview about the oil on the Sunday ranch. A profile of Day-Lewis in ''[[The New York Times Magazine]]'' suggested that original actor Kel O'Neill had been intimidated by Day-Lewis's intensity and habit of staying in character on and off the set.<ref name="Hirschberg" /><ref name="Lewis" /> Anderson, Day-Lewis, and O'Neill all denied this claim,<ref name="Hirschberg" /><ref name="Lewis" /><ref name="Jones-2017">{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Nate |date=December 8, 2017 |title=Did Daniel Day-Lewis Really Freak Out His Co-star on There Will Be Blood? |url=https://www.vulture.com/2017/12/why-kel-oneill-really-left-there-will-be-blood.html |access-date=July 12, 2022 |website=Vulture |language=en-us}}</ref> and Day-Lewis stated, "I absolutely don't believe that it was because he was intimidated by me. I happen to believe that—and I hope I'm right."<ref>{{cite news |last=Longsdorf |first=Amy |title=In 'Blood,' Day-Lewis unearths an oil tycoon's complexities |newspaper=The Morning Call |date=January 3, 2008 |url=https://www.mcall.com/entertainment/movies/all-go_movies.6208480jan03,0,5814474.story |access-date=December 31, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080115004440/http://www.mcall.com/entertainment/movies/all-go_movies.6208480jan03,0,5814474.story |archive-date=January 15, 2008 }}</ref> O'Neill ascribed his dismissal to a poor working relationship with Anderson and his diminished interest in acting.<ref name="Jones-2017" />

Anderson first saw Dano in ''[[The Ballad of Jack and Rose]]'' and thought that he would be perfect to play Paul Sunday, a role he originally envisioned to be a 12 or 14-year-old boy. Dano only had four days to prepare for the much larger role of Eli Sunday,<ref name="National Public Radio Audio Interview, January 8, 2008">{{cite news |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=17926946 |title=National Public Radio Audio Interview |publisher=NPR.org |access-date=November 18, 2012 |archive-date=June 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120615190319/http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=17926946 |url-status=live }}</ref> but he researched the time period that the film is set in as well as [[Evangelism|evangelical]] preachers.<ref name="Stern" /> The previous two weeks of scenes with Sunday and Plainview had to be re-shot with Dano instead of O'Neill.<ref name="Hirschberg" />

The interior mansion scenes were filmed at the [[Greystone Mansion]] in [[Beverly Hills]], the former real-life home of Edward Doheny Jr., a gift from his father, [[Edward Doheny]]. Scenes filmed at Greystone involved the careful renovation of the basement's two-lane bowling alley.<ref name="LATimesHobart">{{cite news |last=Hobart |first=Christy |title=At Greystone, there will be 'Blood' – and bowling |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |pages=F1, F4 |date=December 27, 2007 |url=https://www.latimes.com/features/home/la-hm-blood27dec27,1,6977925.story?ctrack=2&cset=true |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080119060955/http://www.latimes.com/features/home/la-hm-blood27dec27,1,6977925.story?ctrack=2&cset=true <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=January 19, 2008}}</ref> Anderson said it was "a particular situation, because it was so narrow that there could only be a very limited number of people at any given time, maybe five or six behind the camera and then the two boys."<ref name="Modell" /> Day-Lewis later broke a rib in a fall during filming.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Pinewood Dialogue with Daniel Day-Lewis and Paul Thomas Anderson (Transcript) |url=http://www.movingimagesource.us/files/dialogues/2/96175_programs_transcript_html_296.htm |date=December 11, 2007 |access-date=February 21, 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110109160931/http://www.movingimagesource.us/files/dialogues/2/96175_programs_transcript_html_296.htm |work=Museum of the Moving Image |archive-date=January 9, 2011 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Anderson dedicated the film to [[Robert Altman]], who died during editing.<ref name="Stern" />

=== Music ===
{{Further|There Will Be Blood (soundtrack)}}
Anderson had been a fan of [[Radiohead]]'s music and was impressed with [[Jonny Greenwood]]'s scoring of the film ''[[Bodysong]]''. While writing the script for ''There Will Be Blood'', Anderson heard Greenwood's orchestral piece "Popcorn Superhet Receiver", which prompted him to ask Greenwood to work with him. After initially agreeing to score the film, Greenwood had doubts and thought about backing out, but Anderson's reassurance and enthusiasm for the film convinced him to continue.<ref name="Willman">{{cite magazine |last=Willman |first=Chris |title=There Will Be Music |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |date=December 2007 |url=https://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20155516_20155530_20158721,00.html |access-date=December 21, 2007 |archive-date=December 30, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071230001158/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20155516_20155530_20158721,00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Ponto">{{cite news |last=Ponto |first=Arya |title=Jonny Greenwood scoring PTA's new film |work=Just Press Play |date=September 7, 2007 |url=http://www.justpressplay.net/movies/there-will-be-blood/news/radioheads-jonny-greenwood-scoring-ptas-new-film.html |access-date=December 21, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926235832/http://www.justpressplay.net/movies/there-will-be-blood/news/radioheads-jonny-greenwood-scoring-ptas-new-film.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=September 26, 2007}}</ref> Anderson gave Greenwood a copy of the film and three weeks later he came back with two hours of music recorded at [[Abbey Road Studios]] in London.<ref name="Stern" /> Concerning his approach to composing the soundtrack, Greenwood said to ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'':

{{blockquote|I think it was about not necessarily just making period music, which very traditionally you would do. But because they were traditional orchestral sounds, I suppose that's what we hoped was a little unsettling, even though you know all the sounds you're hearing are coming from very old technology. You can just do things with the classical orchestra that do unsettle you, that are sort of slightly wrong, that have some kind of undercurrent that's slightly sinister.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/extendedplay/2007/11/after-a-screeni.html |last=Martens |first=Todd |title=Radiohead's Greenwood goes sinister for 'There Will Be Blood' |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=May 25, 2010 |archive-date=December 6, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091206073938/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/extendedplay/2007/11/after-a-screeni.html |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

In December 2008, Greenwood's score was nominated for a Grammy in the category of "Best Score Soundtrack Album for Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media" for the [[51st Grammy Awards]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://content.grammy.com/grammy_awards/51st_show/list.aspx#22 |title=51st Grammy Awards Nomination List |year=2008 |work=Grammy.com |access-date=January 2, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081205000233/http://content.grammy.com/grammy_awards/51st_show/list.aspx#22 |archive-date=December 5, 2008 }}</ref> It features classical music, such as the third movement ("Vivace Non Troppo") of [[Johannes Brahms]]'s [[Violin Concerto (Brahms)|Violin Concerto in D Major]] and [[Arvo Pärt]]'s "[[Fratres]]" for cello and piano.<ref>{{Citation|title=There Will Be Blood (2007) – IMDb|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0469494/soundtrack|access-date=April 14, 2020|archive-date=October 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201009204504/https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0469494/soundtrack|url-status=live}}</ref>

Greenwood's score was awarded the [[Silver Bear for Outstanding Artistic Contribution]] (music) at the [[58th Berlin International Film Festival]] in 2008.<ref>[https://www.berlinale.de/en/archiv/jahresarchive/2008/03_preistr_ger_2008/03_Preistraeger_2008.html Berlinale. Archiv. Prize winners 2008] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190321010341/https://www.berlinale.de/en/archiv/jahresarchive/2008/03_preistr_ger_2008/03_Preistraeger_2008.html |date=March 21, 2019 }}. Retrieved January 27, 2019.</ref>

== Release ==
=== Box office performance ===
The first public screening of ''There Will Be Blood'' was on September 29, 2007, at [[Fantastic Fest]] in [[Austin, Texas]]. The film was released on December 26, 2007, in New York City and Los Angeles where it grossed [[US$]]190,739 on its opening weekend. The film then opened in 885 theaters in selected markets on January 25, 2008, grossing $4.8&nbsp;million on its opening weekend. The film went on to make $40.2&nbsp;million in North America and $36&nbsp;million in the rest of the world, with a worldwide total of $76.2&nbsp;million, well above its $25&nbsp;million budget;<ref name="BoxOfficeMojo" /> however, the prints and advertising cost for the film's United States release cost about $40&nbsp;million.<ref name="EW.com">[https://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20181242,00.html "EW.com"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131104012830/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20181242,00.html |date=November 4, 2013 }}. Retrieved November 18, 2012.</ref>

=== Home media ===
The film was released on DVD on April 8, 2008.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.awardsdaily.com/2008/03/11/there-will-be-no-commentary/#more-65 |title=There Will Be No Commentary |access-date=March 11, 2008 |work=Awards Daily |date=March 11, 2008 |archive-date=January 13, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160113184106/http://www.awardsdaily.com/2008/03/11/there-will-be-no-commentary/#more-65 |url-status=live }}</ref> An [[HD DVD]] release was announced, but later canceled due to the discontinuation of the format. A [[Blu-ray]] edition was released on June 3, 2008.<ref name="The-Numbers">{{cite web |title=There Will Be Blood |url=https://www.the-numbers.com/movies/2007/TWBLD.php |work=The-Numbers.com |access-date=November 6, 2009 |archive-date=March 9, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090309062012/http://www.the-numbers.com/movies/2007/TWBLD.php |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Reception and legacy ==
=== Critical response ===
On [[review aggregator]] [[Rotten Tomatoes]], ''There Will Be Blood'' has an approval rating of 92% based on 241 reviews, with an average rating of 8.8/10. The website's critical consensus reads, "Widely touted as a masterpiece, this sparse and sprawling epic about the underhanded 'heroes' of capitalism boasts incredible performances by leads Daniel Day-Lewis and Paul Dano, and is director Paul Thomas Anderson's best work to date."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/there_will_be_blood |title=There Will Be Blood |access-date=May 28, 2021 |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Fandango Media|Fandango]] |archive-date=June 5, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200605005923/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/there_will_be_blood |url-status=live }}</ref>
On [[Metacritic]], the film has a [[weighted average]] score of 93 out of 100, based on 42 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.metacritic.com/film/titles/therewillbeblood |title=There Will Be Blood |access-date=March 5, 2008 |work=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=CBS Interactive |archive-date=March 5, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080305155206/http://www.metacritic.com/film/titles/therewillbeblood |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Andrew Sarris]] called the film "an impressive achievement in its confident expertness in rendering the simulated realities of a bygone time and place, largely with an inspired use of regional amateur actors and extras with all the right moves and sounds."<ref name="Sarris">{{cite news |last=Sarris |first=Andrew |title=Oil, Oil Everywhere! |work=New York Observer |date=December 17, 2007 }}</ref> In ''[[Premiere (magazine)|Premiere]]'', [[Glenn Kenny]] praised Day-Lewis's performance: "Once his Plainview takes wing, the relentless focus of the performance makes the character unique."<ref name="Kenny">{{cite news |last=Kenny |first=Glenn |title=There Will Be Blood |work=Premiere.com |date=December 13, 2007 |url=http://www.premiere.com/moviereviews/4316/there-will-be-blood.html |access-date=December 31, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071229223706/http://www.premiere.com/moviereviews/4316/there-will-be-blood.html |archive-date=December 29, 2007 }}</ref> [[Manohla Dargis]] wrote, in her review for ''[[The New York Times]]'', "the film is above all a consummate work of art, one that transcends the historically fraught context of its making, and its pleasures are unapologetically aesthetic."<ref name="Dargis">{{cite news |last=Dargis |first=Manohla |title=An American Primitive, Forged in a Crucible of Blood and Oil |work=The New York Times |date=December 26, 2007 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/26/movies/26bloo.html?ref=movies |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-date=December 8, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201208024919/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/26/movies/26bloo.html?ref=movies |url-status=live }}</ref>

''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]'' praised Day-Lewis's performance: "what's most fun, albeit in a frightening way, is watching this greedmeister become more and more unhinged as he locks horns with Eli Sunday ... both Anderson and Day-Lewis go for broke. But it's a pleasure to be reminded, if only once every four years, that subtlety can be overrated."<ref name="Dangelo">{{cite news |last=D'Angelo |first=Mike |title=One Fine Ham |work=Esquire.com |date=December 26, 2007 |url=https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/movies/a4026/danieldaylewis0108/ |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-date=December 8, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201208024857/https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/movies/a4026/danieldaylewis0108/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Richard Schickel]] in ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' praised ''There Will Be Blood'' as "one of the most wholly original American movies ever made."<ref name="Schickel">{{cite magazine |last=Schickel |first=Richard |title='There Will Be Blood': An American Tragedy |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date=December 24, 2007 |url=https://time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1698168,00.html |access-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-date=December 29, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071229085527/http://www.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1698168,00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Critic Tom Charity, writing about [[CNN]]'s ten-best films list, calls the film the only "flat-out masterpiece" of 2007.<ref name="Charity">{{cite news |title=Review: The best (and worst) films of 2007 |work=CNN |date=December 29, 2007 |author-last1=Charity|author-first1= Tom |access-date=January 6, 2008 |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2007/SHOWBIZ/Movies/12/28/best.2007/ |archive-date=December 31, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071231163842/http://edition.cnn.com/2007/SHOWBIZ/Movies/12/28/best.2007/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Schickel also named the film one of the Top 10 Movies of 2007, ranking it at No. 9, calling Daniel Day-Lewis's performance "astonishing", and calling the film "a mesmerizing meditation on the American spirit in all its maddening ambiguities: mean and noble, angry and secretive, hypocritical and more than a little insane in its aspirations."<ref>[[Schickel, Richard]]: [https://time.com/time/specials/2007/top10/article/0,30583,1686204_1686244_1692274,00.html "The 10 Best Movies"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090430061710/http://www.time.com/time/specials/2007/top10/article/0,30583,1686204_1686244_1692274,00.html |date=April 30, 2009 }}; Time.com.</ref> James Christopher, chief film critic for ''[[The Times]]'', published a list in April 2008 of his top 100 films, placing ''There Will Be Blood'' in second place, behind only ''[[Casablanca (film)|Casablanca]]''.<ref>{{cite news |first=James |last=Christopher |title=Top 100 Films |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/related_features/top_100_films |work=The Times |date=April 27, 2008 |location=London |access-date=April 27, 2008 |archive-date=May 2, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080502064232/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/related_features/top_100_films/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Some critics were positive toward the work but less laudatory, often criticizing its ending. [[Mick LaSalle]] of the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'', challenged the film's high praise by saying "there should be no need to pretend ''There Will Be Blood'' is a masterpiece just because Anderson sincerely tried to make it one" and noting that "the scenes between Day-Lewis and Dano ultimately degenerate into a ridiculous [[burlesque]]."<ref name="SFCreview">{{cite news |title=Conquering the West, and getting his hands dirty in the process |work=San Francisco Chronicle |date=January 4, 2008 |author-last1=LaSalle|author-first1= Mick |access-date=April 19, 2008 |url=https://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Conquering-the-West-and-getting-his-hands-dirty-3233876.php |archive-date=September 21, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120921062317/http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Conquering-the-West-and-getting-his-hands-dirty-3233876.php |url-status=live }}</ref> Several months after LaSalle's initial review of the film, he reiterated that while he still did not consider ''There Will Be Blood'' to be a masterpiece, he wondered if its "style, an approach, an attitude... might become important in the future."<ref name="Maximum Strength Mick">{{cite news |title=Winning the Future: Through What Works Will Our Era Be Remembered? |work=San Francisco Chronicle |date=May 12, 2008 |author-last1=LaSalle|author-first1= Mick |access-date=February 15, 2009 |url=https://blog.sfgate.com/mlasalle/2008/05/12/winning-the-future-through-what-works-will-our-era-be-remembered/ |archive-date=November 2, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121102024348/http://blog.sfgate.com/mlasalle/2008/05/12/winning-the-future-through-what-works-will-our-era-be-remembered/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Roger Ebert]] assigned the film three and a half out of four stars and wrote, "''There Will Be Blood'' is the kind of film that is easily called great. I am not sure of its greatness. It was filmed in the same area of Texas used by ''[[No Country for Old Men]]'', and that is a great film, and a perfect one. But ''There Will Be Blood'' is not perfect, and in its imperfections (its unbending characters, its lack of women or any reflection of ordinary society, its ending, its relentlessness) we may see its reach exceeding its grasp. Which is not a dishonorable thing."<ref>{{cite news | title=''There Will Be Blood'' review – Roger Ebert | url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/there-will-be-blood-2008 | work=Chicago Sun-Times | date=January 4, 2008 | access-date=February 19, 2021 | archive-date=January 20, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120171540/https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/there-will-be-blood-2008 | url-status=live }}</ref>

Carla Meyer of the ''[[Sacramento Bee]]'', who gave the film the same star rating as Ebert, opined that the final confrontation between Daniel and Eli marked when the work "stops being a masterpiece and becomes a really good movie. What was grand becomes petty, then overwrought."<ref>{{cite news |title=Movie review: Brutally real – Daniel Day Lewis exudes authenticity in oil-field drama 'There Will Be Blood' |work=The Sacramento Bee |date=January 11, 2008 |author-last1=Meyer|author-first1= Carla |access-date=May 9, 2008 |url=https://www.sacbee.com/meyer/story/623040.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080330141358/http://www.sacbee.com/meyer/story/623040.html |archive-date=March 30, 2008}}</ref> In 2014, Peter Walker of ''[[The Guardian]]'' likewise argued that the scene "might not be the very worst scene in the history of recent Oscar-garlanded cinema ... but it's perhaps the one most inflated with its own delusional self-importance."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2014/nov/12/there-will-be-blood-my-most-overrated-film |title=There Will be Blood: my most overrated film |last=Walker |first=Peter |newspaper=The Guardian |date=November 12, 2014 |access-date=January 29, 2017 |archive-date=February 2, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202135535/https://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2014/nov/12/there-will-be-blood-my-most-overrated-film |url-status=live }}</ref>

Since 2008, the film has been included in the book ''[[1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die]]'' and every revised edition released afterwards.<ref>{{cite book |last=Schneider |first=Stephen Jay |title=1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die |publisher=Octopus Publishing Group, London |date=April 10, 2010 |pages=928 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a1MSRAAACAAJ&q=1001+movies+you+must+see+before+you+die |isbn=978-1-84403-690-5 |access-date=September 23, 2012}}</ref> ''[[Total Film]]'' placed it at number three in their list of the 50 best movies of ''Total Film''{{'s}} lifetime.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/50-best-movies-of-total-film-magazine-s-lifetime/|title=Total Film – GamesRadar+|access-date=January 11, 2017|archive-date=January 31, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170131004215/http://www.gamesradar.com/50-best-movies-of-total-film-magazine-s-lifetime/|url-status=live}}</ref> In ''[[The Guardian]]'', journalist Steve Rose ranked it the 17th best arthouse film of all time, and in a separate 2019 ranking a panel of four ''Guardian'' journalists ranked it the best film of the 21st century.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/oct/20/there-will-blood-anderson-arthouse|title=There Will Be Blood: No 17 best arthouse film of all time|author-first1=Steve |author-last1=Rose|work=the Guardian|date=October 20, 2010 |access-date=December 13, 2016|archive-date=January 16, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170116202223/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/oct/20/there-will-blood-anderson-arthouse|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The 100 best films of the 21st century |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/sep/13/100-best-films-movies-of-the-21st-century |website=The Guardian |date=September 13, 2019 |access-date=September 17, 2019 |archive-date=June 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200622105737/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/sep/13/100-best-films-movies-of-the-21st-century |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2024, filmmaker [[Quentin Tarantino]] named it one of the best films of the 21st century, although, in the following year, [[Quentin Tarantino#Altercations with industry peers|he criticized Dano's performance]]  and instead wanted to replace Austin Butler as a better choice if he had to pick the best.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/quentin-tarantino-favourite-21st-century-movies/|title=Quentin Tarantino names the best 21st century movies|date=November 4, 2024|website=faroutmagazine.co.uk}}</ref>

=== Top ten lists ===
The film was on the [[American Film Institute]]'s Top 10 Movies of the Year; AFI's jury said:

<blockquote>
''There Will Be Blood'' is bravura film-making by one of American film's modern masters. Paul Thomas Anderson's epic poem of savagery, optimism and obsession is a true meditation on America. The film drills down into the dark heart of capitalism, where domination, not gain, is the ultimate goal. In a career defined by transcendent performances, Daniel Day-Lewis creates a character so rich and so towering, that "Daniel Plainview" will haunt the history of film for generations to come.<ref>[https://www.afi.com/tvevents/afiawards07/movies07.aspx "AFI Movies of the Year Official Selections"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605081634/http://www.afi.com/tvevents/afiawards07/movies07.aspx |date=2011-06-05 }}. ''American Film Institute''. Retrieved November 18, 2012.</ref>
</blockquote>

The film appeared on many critics' top ten lists of the best films of 2007.<ref name="Metacritic07-Top10">{{cite web |url=https://www.metacritic.com/film/awards/2007/toptens.shtml |title=Metacritic: 2007 Film Critic Top Ten Lists |access-date=January 5, 2008 |work=Metacritic |publisher=CBS Interactive |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080102102034/http://www.metacritic.com/film/awards/2007/toptens.shtml <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=January 2, 2008}}</ref><ref name="MovieCityNews">{{cite web |url=https://moviecitynews.com/awards/2008/top_ten/00index.html |title=Movie City News: 2007 Film Critic Top Ten Lists |access-date=January 8, 2008 |work=Movie City News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080103085851/http://www.moviecitynews.com/awards/2008/top_ten/00index.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date=January 3, 2008}}</ref>

=== Decade-end lists ===
Review aggregator site [[Metacritic]], when comparing over 40 'top ten of the decade' lists from various notable publications, found ''There Will Be Blood'' to be the most mentioned, appearing on 46% of critics' lists and being ranked the decade's best film on five of them.

In December 2009, Peter Travers of ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' chose the film as the No. 1 film of the decade, saying:
<blockquote>Two years after first seeing ''There Will Be Blood'', I am convinced that Paul Thomas Anderson's profound portrait of an American primitive—take that, ''[[Citizen Kane]]''—deserves pride of place among the decade's finest. Daniel Day-Lewis gave the best and ballsiest performance of the past 10 years. As Daniel Plainview, a prospector who loots the land of its natural resources in silver and oil to fill his pockets and gargantuan ego, he showed us a man draining his humanity for power. And Anderson, having extended Plainview's rage from Earth to heaven in the form of a corrupt preacher (Paul Dano), managed to "drink the milkshake" of other risk-taking directors. If I had to stake the future of film in the next decade on one filmmaker, I'd go with PTA. Even more than ''[[Boogie Nights]]'' and ''[[Magnolia (film)|Magnolia]]''—his rebel cries from the 1990s—''Blood'' let Anderson put technology at the service of character. The score by [[Radiohead]]'s Jonny Greenwood was a sonic explosion that reinvented what film music could be. And the images captured by Robert Elswit, a genius of camera and lighting, made visual poetry out of an oil well consumed by flame. For the final word on ''Blood'', I'll quote Plainview: "It was one goddamn hell of a show."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/photos/gallery/31234572/peter_travers_10_best_movies_of_t/photo/10ml |title=Peter Travers' 10 Best Movies of the Decade |work=Rolling Stone Magazine |date=December 10, 2009 |access-date=December 10, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100114150503/http://www.rollingstone.com/photos/gallery/31234572/peter_travers_10_best_movies_of_t/photo/10ml |archive-date=January 14, 2010 }}</ref></blockquote>

''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' and ''[[At the Movies (1986 TV program)|At the Movies]]'' critic [[Michael Phillips (critic)|Michael Phillips]] named ''There Will Be Blood'' the decade's best film. Phillips stated:
<blockquote>This most eccentric and haunting of modern epics is driven by oilman Daniel Plainview, who, in the hands of actor Daniel Day-Lewis, becomes a [[Horatio Alger]] story gone horribly wrong. Writer/director Paul Thomas Anderson's camera is as crucial to the film's hypnotic pull as the performance at its center. For its evocation of the early 1900s, its relentless focus on one man's fascinating obsessions, and for its inspiring example of how to freely adapt a novel—plus, what I think is the performance of the new century—''There Will Be Blood'' stands alone. The more I see it, the sadder, and stranger, and more visually astounding it grows—and the more it seems to say about the best and worst in the American ethos of rugged individualism. Awfully good!<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bventertainment.go.com/tv/buenavista/atm/specials/bestofthedecade/index.html |title=Best of the Decade |date=December 28, 2009 |access-date=December 28, 2009}}{{dead link|date=November 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref></blockquote>

''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' critic Lisa Schwarzbaum named ''There Will Be Blood'' the decade's best film as well. In her original review, Schwarzbaum stated:
<blockquote>Anyhow, a fierce story meshing big exterior-oriented themes of American character with an interior-oriented portrait of an impenetrable man (two men, really, including the false prophet Sunday) is only half Anderson's quest, and his exciting achievement. The other half lies in the innovation applied to the telling itself. For a huge picture, ''There Will Be Blood'' is exquisitely intimate, almost a collection of sketches. For a long, slow movie, it speeds. For a story set in the fabled bad-old-days past, it's got the terrors of modernity in its DNA. Leaps of romantic chordal grandeur from Brahms' Violin Concerto in D Major announce the launch of a fortune-changing oil well down the road from Eli Sunday's church—and then, much later, announce a kind of end of the world. For bleakness, the movie can't be beat—nor for brilliance.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20168259,00.html |title=There Will Be Blood Review |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=January 9, 2008 |access-date=January 9, 2008 |archive-date=January 7, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080107070307/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20168259,00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref></blockquote>

In December 2009, the website [[Gawker.com]] determined that ''There Will Be Blood'' is film critics' consensus best film of the decade when aggregating all Best of the Decade lists, stating: "And when the votes were all in, by a nose, ''There Will Be Blood'' stood alone at the top of the decade, its straw in the whole damn cinema's milkshake."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gawker.com/5428998/there-will-be-blood-wins-the-decade |title=There Will Be Blood Wins the Decade |work=Gawker |date=December 18, 2009 |access-date=February 7, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100203203506/http://gawker.com/5428998/there-will-be-blood-wins-the-decade |archive-date=February 3, 2010 }}</ref>

=== Best of the Century lists ===

Filmmakers [[Denis Villeneuve]], [[Antoine Fuqua]], [[Darius Khondji]], [[Cord Jefferson]], [[Joanna Hogg]], [[Reinaldo Marcus Green]], [[Kate Berlant]], [[Josh Safdie]], [[Robert Eggers]] and [[Jason Blum]] have all cited the film as among the best of the 21st century.<ref>{{cite news |title=Denis Villeneuve's Favorite Movies: 29 Films the Director Wants You to See |url=https://www.indiewire.com/gallery/denis-villeneuve-favorite-movies/ |access-date=17 March 2025|work=IndieWire |date=26 February 2023 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://collider.com/directors-pick-best-movies-of-the-21st-century/ | title=Directors Pick Their Favorite Movies of the 21st Century | website=[[Collider (website)|Collider]] | date=June 9, 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/06/09/movies/directors-favorite-movies.html | title=Six Directors Pick Their Favorite Films of the 21st-Century | work=The New York Times | date=June 9, 2017 | last1=Ryzik | first1=Melena }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/votes-movies-21st-century.html | title=Pedro Almódovar, Sofia Coppola and 117 Other Famous Names Share Their Top Movies of the 21st Century | work=The New York Times | date=June 23, 2025 }}</ref>

In 2016, it was voted the number three in the [[BBC's 100 Greatest Films of the 21st Century]] as picked by 177 film critics from around the world.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20160819-the-21st-centurys-100-greatest-films?referer=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2F|title=The 21st Century's 100 greatest films|date=August 23, 2016|access-date=January 11, 2017|archive-date=June 24, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200624122246/https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20160819-the-21st-centurys-100-greatest-films?referer=https%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2F|url-status=live}}</ref> In the same year, the [[Directors Guild of America]] ranked the film 61st on its list of ''The 80 Best-Directed Films'' since the Guild’s founding in 1936.<ref>{{Cite news |title=The 80 Best-Directed Films - |url=https://www.dga.org/craft/dgaq/all-articles/1602-spring-2016/80th-film-poll.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241226110741/https://www.dga.org/craft/dgaq/all-articles/1602-spring-2016/80th-film-poll.aspx |archive-date=2024-12-26 |access-date=2026-10-18 |work=[[Directors Guild of America]] |language=en}}</ref> In 2021, members of [[Writers Guild of America West]] (WGAW) and [[Writers Guild of America, East]] (WGAE) ranked its screenplay 7th in WGA’s 101 Greatest Screenplays of the 21st Century (so far).<ref>{{Cite web |title=101 Greatest Screenplays of the 21st Century (*so far) |url=https://www.wga.org/writers-room/101-best-lists/101-best-screenplays-of-the-21st-century-so-far/list |access-date=2025-12-26 |website=www.wga.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Pedersen |first=Erik |date=2021-12-06 |title=101 Greatest Screenplays Of The 21st Century: Horror Pic Tops Writers Guild’s List |url=https://deadline.com/2021/12/greatest-screenplays-of-21st-century-list-writers-guild-get-out-1234885622/ |access-date=2025-12-26 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref> The film was tied for 122nd place in the 2022 ''[[Sight and Sound]]'' critic's poll.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Greatest Films of All Time |url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/greatest-films-all-time |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=BFI |language=en}}</ref>

In June 2025, the film ranked number three on ''[[The New York Times]]''{{'}} list of "[[NYT's 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century|The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century]]" and ranked number 4 on its "Readers' Choice" edition of the list.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/best-movies-21st-century.html | title=The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century | work=The New York Times | date=June 26, 2025 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Readers Choose Their Top Movies of the 21st Century |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/readers-movies-21st-century.html |website=The New York Times |date=July 2, 2025 |access-date=2 July 2025}}</ref>

In July 2025, ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' ranked ''There Will Be Blood'' as the best movie of the 21st century.<ref>{{cite magazine | url=https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-lists/best-movies-of-the-21st-century-1235200512/ | title=100 Best Movies of the 21st Century | magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] | date=July 1, 2025 }}</ref>
